title: The Exterminating Angel (1962): trenchant and relevant satire

commenti.body:
A few threads of what is on offer here:

**1) The castaway narrative.** This is the most evident thematic parallel, certainly by the end of the salon ordeal. Buñuel had made ***Robinson Crusoe*** in 1950, and was intrigued by the concept of the castaway. The screenplay and working title for the film was "Los Náufragos de la Calle de la Providencia" - the castaways of Providence Street, which appears in the opening credits. Golding's ***Lord of the Flies*** was published in 1954 and the film adaptation would be released a year after The Exterminating Angel.  
  
The slaughter of the sheep that stray into the salon bears some similarities to the hunting and roasting of the boar in Lord of the Flies, showing how far the characters have fallen, but it also acts as a kind of ritual substitute to the human sacrifice that is demanded toward the end. Triangle of Sadness (2022) is a recent example of a castaway drama featuring the same kind of social satire, but made much more obvious and strident.   
  
**2) Anticlericalism.** The original "**Exterminating Angel**" was a 19th century secret society founded in Spain by ultra-conservative Catholic clerics which designated people as pure (orthodox Catholics) or impure (atheistic liberals). The impure were to be exterminated by members of the group, an ancestor to later reactionary terrorist groups and of course the Franco regime itself.   
  
This thematic strand is implanted both by the opening credits, which show a church facade as sacred music plays, and by the ending in which the socialites, freed from their salon prison, are once again trapped along with all the clerics and congregation in a cathedral, as soldiers unleash savage repression outside. The bracketing of church ritual at the start and end of the film might indicate that the movie itself is a kind of ritual, an anti-mass.   
  
**3) Class.** Every viewer can see that class is central to the thematic drive of the film. The lower-classes seem immune to the curse, the servants able and highly anxious to leave, and Julio the butler is also free until he enters the salon.   
  
The upper classes seem utterly free of the bourgeois attitudes to patriotism, honour and sex. The colonel admits that he is frightened of combat and describes the motherland as just a series of rivers that flow into the sea. The only thing that is emphasised, their only value, is decorum, good manners.   
  
A revealing discussion is when the women talk frankly about how little they sympathise with the little people - "It seems to me that the lower class don't suffer pain the way we do". It is explicitly contrasted with the histrionic grief they display at the death of a handsome militaristic princely hero. This lack of basic empathy seems like the karma that causes them to suffer as they do.  
  
**4) The horror genre and the gothic.** The film itself might be seen as a kind of horror film, where the guests struggle on gamely during the daylight hours but revert to a sinister perversity at night. There are dead bodies in closets and a sequence featuring a severed hand as in ***The Beast with Five Fingers*** (1946) but subverted and played for laughs as it was way back in Buñuel's first film, ***Un chien andalou*** (1929).  
  
The gothic genre obsessively strips away the conscious self, leaving the individual a mass of fear and desire, and despite the ironic distance throughout the film, the viewer comes to identify with these desperate people. To some extent we also go through this process of stripping of self, asking what we would do if all social structures of identity were removed. Would we also transgress as they do? Would we also shit in a jar, strip a lamb to shreds, and steal dope? 

\[Extracted from my [full review](https://letterboxd.com/hootsmaguire/film/the-exterminating-angel/) \]

I am not convinced that it’s an allegory for Franco’s Spain. I consider it to be primarily an allegory for how the upper class becomes isolated from the working class an unable to connect with/relate to them. I feel like if it was about Franco there would’ve been a clear leader/victor in the end. There also aren’t any themes relating to left or right winged ideology. There are, however, lots of themes relating to class and class divide. It isn’t until the end, when the upper class are reduced to drinking water from leaking pipes and eating sheep they slaughtered themselves are they able to reconnect with the rest of the world.
